title: Insurance submission workflow improvement: a CUO's guide to optimizing submission ingestion
summary: Insurance submission workflow improvement for CUOs: five ingestion measures, a stage-by-stage workflow and a 90-day plan to lift capacity and hit ratio.
body_markdown:
Insurance submission workflow improvement starts with a simple decision for a chief underwriting officer: run submission ingestion, the[submission intake](https://www.pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/submission-intake) work that turns a broker's email and attachments into a file an underwriter can act on, as a measured operation with its own targets, because ingestion decides how much underwriter time reaches risk selection and how quickly brokers hear back. Most desks still treat ingestion as clerical work that sits before underwriting, and the numbers show why that view has become expensive. According to the[WSIA midyear report, covered by Business Insurance in August 2026](https://www.businessinsurance.com/surplus-lines-premium-growth-slows-sharply-in-first-half-of-2026/) , surplus lines item filings rose 16.9% in the first half of 2026 while premium rose only 2.8%, which means each filing now brings in about 12% less premium than it did a year earlier. At the same time, the[Capgemini World Property and Casualty Insurance Report 2024](https://www.capgemini.com/insights/research-library/unleashing-growth-the-evolving-role-of-underwriters/) found that commercial underwriters spend 41% to 43% of their time on administrative work such as data entry and record keeping. A desk that reads more files for less premium, with almost half its time spent on keying data, carries a cost problem that no rate plan will solve. This guide sets out the five measures we think a CUO should own, what an optimized ingestion workflow looks like stage by stage, and how to sequence the work over a quarter.


## Why should a CUO own submission ingestion?


A CUO should own ingestion because it sets the ceiling on how much risk selection the desk can do and how quickly brokers hear back on every account that follows. Underwriting results are usually explained through rate, selection and claims, yet each of those depends on what happens in the first hours after a broker hits send. When ingestion runs slowly, the best accounts are often placed elsewhere before an underwriter opens them. When ingestion runs carelessly, a misread field flows into rating and the error shows up months later as a reserve or an audit finding. Consider an illustrative desk of 30 underwriters. Using the Capgemini split, about 42% of their time, or 12.6 full-time equivalents, goes to administrative work, and about 33%, or 9.9 full-time equivalents, goes to core risk work. If better ingestion cuts the administrative share to 20%, the desk gets back 6.6 full-time equivalents and its core underwriting time rises to 16.5, roughly two-thirds more risk selection from the same headcount. That gain is the reason ingestion belongs on the CUO's scorecard, alongside the[combined ratio](https://www.pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/combined-ratio) it eventually moves. Our earlier analysis of why[submission volume is rising while underwriting capacity is not](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/underwriting-capacity-submissions-rising) shows how quickly that gap widens in a growing book.


## Which five measures show whether submission ingestion is working?


Five measures tell a CUO whether ingestion is healthy, and each one ties to a part of the underwriting P&L. Most carriers and MGAs track only volume and turnaround, which hides the stages where time is lost and errors begin. We suggest a short scorecard of five measures, reviewed monthly by line of business, so that each owner can see which stage is holding the desk back. A scorecard like this also changes the conversation with the operations team, since every improvement request can point at a measure and a baseline instead of a general sense that the inbox is slow. It gives the CFO a way to see ingestion as a cost line, and it gives distribution leaders a number to share with brokers. The table below sets out each measure, what it tells you, the failure it usually exposes and a sensible target.


Measure What it tells you Common failure Target to set


**Time to first decision** Whether brokers hear back while the account is still in play Submissions wait in a shared inbox in arrival order Clear, decline or request information the same business day


**Completeness at first touch** Share of submissions with every required document on arrival Missing loss runs found by the underwriter days later Missing items flagged and requested within 15 minutes


**Workflow accuracy** Share of submissions whose extracted data matches the source documents from intake through rating Errors found only at rating, audit or claim 99.9% workflow accuracy with a human-in-the-loop review step


**Clearance and appetite accuracy** Share of accounts correctly cleared, declined or routed Out-of-appetite accounts reach senior underwriters Every decline traced to a written appetite rule


**Handling cost per premium dollar** What ingestion costs as a share of premium written Cost tracked per head with no link to submissions Reported monthly for each line of business


The first two measures protect the hit ratio, the middle two protect pricing and risk selection, and the last one protects the expense side of the combined ratio. A desk that improves only speed tends to move errors downstream faster, while a desk that improves only accuracy tends to lose brokers to quicker markets, so the five measures work best as a set. We suggest that each measure has a named owner, a baseline taken from a sample of recent submissions, and a target agreed with the heads of each line of business. Reviewing them together every month shows where a gain in one stage has created a delay or an error in the next, which is the most common way ingestion projects disappoint. It also keeps the program honest, since a measure that never moves is a signal that the change has not reached the desk.


## How does slow ingestion cost quotes a carrier wants to win?


Slow ingestion loses good business because brokers now choose carriers by how easy it is to submit. According to the[2026 Insurance Agency-Carrier Connectivity Trends report from Ivans, reported by Insurance Business in August 2026](https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/breaking-news/submission-friction-now-beats-price-in-where-agents-place-business-ivans-finds-587645.aspx) , 90% of agents have reduced business with a carrier because of submission friction, and submission friction has overtaken product and price as the main factor in where agents place business. The same research found that 79% of agents rank commercial submission automation as the capability they most want from carriers, while 49% of commercial-heavy agencies still rely on email to send submissions. That combination matters for a CUO, since the market is asking for speed while most submissions still arrive as unstructured emails with attachments. A carrier that needs three days to open, sort and key an email submission gives a faster competitor three days to quote the account first. Our look at[submission turnaround time in commercial P&C](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/submission-turnaround-time-commercial-pc) explains why slow intake loses more business than pricing does, our guide to[broker email submission extraction](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/broker-email-submission-extraction-commercial-pc-first-mile) covers the email first mile in detail, and our overview of[submission intake automation for commercial P&C](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/submission-intake-automation-commercial-p-and-c) sets out what carriers should expect from the tools that handle it.


## What does a field error at intake cost later in the workflow?


A field error at intake costs the most of any error, since every later step trusts the number it was given. Rating engines, referral rules and pricing models all assume that the payroll, revenue, total insured value or prior losses on the screen match the documents the broker sent. Take an illustrative workers' compensation account with $4.2M of payroll and a rate of $3.00 per $100 of payroll, which should produce $126,000 of premium. If the payroll is keyed as $2.4M, the quote drops to $72,000, a shortfall of $54,000, or about 43%, that no later rate change will recover for the policy term. If the error runs the other way, the quote is too high and the broker places the account with another market, so the carrier loses a risk it wanted. Both outcomes start with one transposed digit at ingestion. This is why we suggest measuring accuracy against the source documents for every field that drives rating, with a human reviewer checking any value the AI flags as uncertain. Our research on[the real cost of inaccurate underwriting data](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/real-cost-inaccurate-underwriting-data-commercial-p-c) shows how these errors compound across a book.


## What does an optimized submission ingestion workflow look like, stage by stage?


An optimized ingestion workflow moves each submission through five clear stages, each with an owner and a measure. The stages are familiar to most underwriting operations teams, yet in many carriers and MGAs they run as manual handoffs between assistants, analysts and underwriters, with no clock running on any of them. That lack of a clock is the real problem, because a submission can sit for a day between two people without anyone noticing, and the delay only becomes visible when a broker calls to chase the quote. Giving every stage a timestamp and an owner turns those hidden waits into numbers a manager can act on, and it shows which handoff deserves automation first. The table compares a common current state with an optimized one and shows which scorecard measure each stage moves.


Stage Common state today Optimized state Measure it moves


**Capture** Email, portal and API submissions tracked in separate places Every channel lands in one queue with a timestamp Time to first decision


**Classify** Staff open each attachment to see what it is ACORD forms, loss runs, schedules and supplementals labeled on arrival Completeness at first touch


**Extract and verify** Fields re-keyed into rating and admin systems Fields extracted, checked against the source and reviewed by a person where confidence is low Workflow accuracy


**Complete and clear** Gaps and duplicates found by the underwriter days later Missing items requested from the broker within minutes; duplicates and clearance conflicts caught Completeness and clearance accuracy


**Triage and route** Worked in arrival order Ranked by appetite fit, broker hit ratio and account quality, then sent to the right desk Time to first decision and handling cost


Pibit AI's agents run this sequence across the[Intake & clearance](https://www.pibit.ai/intake-and-clearance) , Extraction & research and Triage & risk analysis stages of the AI Underwriting OS, with our human-in-the-loop holding 99.9% workflow accuracy, on top of the policy administration systems carriers already use. Pibit AI works with 50+ carriers and MGAs across 10+ lines of business, and the pattern we see most often is that the biggest early gain comes from the complete-and-clear stage, where missing documents and duplicate submissions quietly consume underwriter hours. Catching those problems before a file reaches an underwriter removes rework that most desks never measure. Each stage can be improved on its own, so a carrier can start with the stage that hurts most and add the others as the scorecard shows results. The[submission clearance](https://www.pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/submission-clearance) entry in our insurance knowledge library explains the clearance step in more detail.


## Where should automation stop and an underwriter take over?


Automation should stop at the point where a decision needs judgment about the risk itself. Capturing, sorting, extracting and checking documents are tasks with a right answer that can be verified against the source, so they suit AI agents with human review on uncertain fields. Deciding whether a contractor's growth story is credible, whether a loss trend reflects bad luck or bad controls, or whether to stretch appetite for a strategic broker are judgments that belong with an experienced underwriter. A good ingestion workflow makes that boundary explicit and visible to everyone on the desk, so that nobody has to guess which steps a machine has already checked. In our view the following decisions should stay with an underwriter, even when the data arrives clean and complete:


- Accepting an account that sits at the edge of written appetite or needs a referral.
- Reading a loss history for causes that the numbers alone do not explain.
- Setting terms, conditions and pricing adjustments that depart from the rating model.
- Handling a broker relationship where the account is part of a wider program.


Drawing the line this way gives the underwriter a prepared file and a clear question to answer, which is the best use of scarce senior time. It also makes the workflow easier to defend when a regulator or auditor asks how a decision was made, since every automated step has a source document behind it and every judgment has a named underwriter attached. Carriers that blur this boundary tend to end up with one of two problems, either underwriters who re-check every extracted field because they do not trust the data, or automated declines that nobody can explain to a broker. A clear handoff point avoids both, and it gives the desk a simple rule that new underwriters can learn in their first week. Senior underwriters, in turn, spend their time on the accounts where experience changes the outcome.


## How should a CUO sequence ingestion improvements over 90 days?


A CUO can improve ingestion in about one quarter by fixing measurement first and automation second. The temptation is to start with the most visible pain, usually the email inbox, yet without a baseline nobody can tell whether a change helped or simply moved work elsewhere. We suggest four steps, each lasting a few weeks, run on one line of business before the approach is extended. Starting with one line keeps the sample manageable, gives the team a quick and visible result, and creates an internal reference case that makes the next line easier to change. A line with high submission volume and a moderate average premium, such as a small commercial package or a workers' compensation program, usually shows the clearest results in the shortest time. The plan below assumes a desk that already has written appetite rules for that line:


- **Weeks 1 to 3, baseline the five measures.** Sample a month of submissions and record time to first decision, completeness, workflow accuracy, clearance accuracy and handling cost.
- **Weeks 4 to 6, fix completeness and clearance.** Flag missing documents on arrival, request them from brokers automatically and catch duplicates before an underwriter opens the file, following the[submission intake best practices](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/submission-intake-best-practices-commercial-pc) we have set out for commercial P&C.
- **Weeks 7 to 9, verify fields at the source.** Extract and check the fields that drive rating, with human review on uncertain values, and track workflow accuracy weekly.
- **Weeks 10 to 13, route by appetite and value.** Replace arrival-order queues with ranking by appetite fit and broker hit ratio, then compare the scorecard with the baseline.


With premium per filing falling, as the WSIA data shows, and commercial premiums down 2% on average in the second quarter of 2026 according to the[CIAB market survey reported by Insurance Journal](https://insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/08/20/882240.htm) , a quarter spent on ingestion is one of the few levers that lowers cost and raises hit ratio at the same time. Our analysis of[E&S submission volume as a throughput problem](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/es-submission-volume-soft-rates-throughput-problem) explains why that lever matters most in a softening market. In our view, a carrier or MGA that can quote its cost per submission, completeness rate and workflow accuracy as readily as its rate change will be in a far stronger position when the cycle turns, and one quarter of measurement on a single line is enough to get those numbers on the table.
